source: Green (2005) Game theory, simulated interaction, and unaided judgement for forecasting decisions in conflicts: Further evidence, Int J Forecasting 21
finding: In eight real conflicts, game theorists forecast no better than novices using plain judgement. Role-playing by students was twice as accurate.
numbers: 101 forecasts by 23 game theorists: 31% correct. 354 unaided student forecasts: 31%. 105 simulated-interaction forecasts: 62%, average error reduction 47% vs game theorists. 8 conflicts (5 earlier plus 3 new chosen to suit game theory).
quote: Game theory experts were no more accurate than novices.
limits: Eight conflicts is small. Choice of conflicts may not be representative. Forecast was a pick from a list.
agent_relevance: Playing the other side out beats a single expert opinion about the other side. Supports a separate opponent role in wargaming, with the opponent role-played in full.

source: Green (2005) Game theory, simulated interaction, and unaided judgement for forecasting decisions in conflicts: Further evidence, Int J Forecasting 21
finding: Simulated interaction beat game theory in all 8 conflicts. The gain does not depend on how easy the conflict was.
numbers: Permutation test P=0.004 (one-tailed, paired, 8 conflicts). Four easiest conflicts (49% correct by game theorists): error cut 49%. Four hardest (13% correct): error cut 45%.
limits: Same small set of 8 conflicts. Conflicts from the same research group.
agent_relevance: The opponent-play advantage held for easy and hard cases, so it is not a ceiling effect.

source: Green (2005) Game theory, simulated interaction, and unaided judgement for forecasting decisions in conflicts: Further evidence, Int J Forecasting 21
finding: Expertise, experience and effort did not help. Experienced game theorists were not more accurate, and neither were those who spent more time.
numbers: Game theorists 31% vs novices 31%. Median expectation of 77 people before the data: novice judgement 30%, simulated interaction 40%, game theorists 50%.
limits: Expectations came from 77 respondents at talks; not the target population of decision makers.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a single expert-style persona to predict an adversary. A model should not treat its own confident forecast as strong evidence (links to G4).

source: Green (2005) Game theory, simulated interaction, and unaided judgement for forecasting decisions in conflicts: Further evidence, Int J Forecasting 21
finding: Combining several simulated-interaction runs gave an accurate forecast in 7 of 8 situations.
numbers: 7 of 8 situations accurate when forecasts were combined; single forecasts 62%.
limits: Combining rule and sample size were small. Eight situations only.
agent_relevance: Run the adversary role several times and aggregate in code. This fits the schema rule that code selects (G5).

source: Green (2005) Game theory, simulated interaction, and unaided judgement for forecasting decisions in conflicts: Further evidence, Int J Forecasting 21
finding: Usefulness ratings gave the same ranking as accuracy.
numbers: Mean usefulness on a 10-point scale: simulated interaction 6.6, game theorists 4.3, random choice 4.1. Rater agreement was modest (kappa 0.249, P<0.001, 5 raters).
limits: Five convenience raters. Modest agreement.
agent_relevance: Even a wrong forecast from role-play can be useful; score a wargame by usefulness as well as exact hits.

source: Armstrong (2002) Assessing game theory, role playing, and unaided judgment, Int J Forecasting 18
finding: Armstrong's audit of Green (2002): the design favoured game theory, yet role playing still won. The effect concentrates where parties interact.
numbers: Excluding the one non-interactive case: chance, unaided judgement and game theory about 28% correct each; role playing 61%. Role playing had half the error of unaided judgement. Wilcoxon one-tailed P=0.03 for 6 situations. Over 1100 participants. Error reduction 48% on the three easiest and 50% on the three hardest situations.
quote: Role playing was substantially more accurate than game theory despite biases favoring game theory.
limits: Excluding Panalba was a post-hoc choice by the commentator. Role-players were mostly students who may not have taken it seriously. Armstrong called for replication by sceptics.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: opponent role-play helps when the outcome comes from interaction between parties. For a decision with no counter-actor, other tests may do as well.

source: Armstrong (2002) Assessing game theory, role playing, and unaided judgment, Int J Forecasting 18
finding: In the single non-interactive situation (Panalba Drug Policy), game theory beat role playing.
numbers: Game theory better than role playing in 1 of 6 situations, the one with no interaction between parties.
limits: One case.
agent_relevance: A wargame step should be used only when an adversary or a reacting party exists.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making (FAccT)
finding: Eight LLM nation agents in a 14-day crisis game escalated. None of 5 models showed a statistically significant de-escalation in any of 3 scenarios.
numbers: 5 models, 3 scenarios (neutral, invasion, cyberattack), 10 runs each, 8 agents, 27 actions. All models showed a significant initial escalation. GPT-3.5 neutral scenario score rose from 10.15 to 26.02 (+256%).
quote: None of our five models across all three scenarios exhibit statistically significant de-escalation across the duration of our simulations.
limits: Simulation is simplified. Escalation score is a design choice. Only 10 runs per cell. Sampling temperature non-zero adds noise. World model was GPT-3.5.
agent_relevance: One model on all sides drifts toward escalation. An adversary played by the same model as the planner will not be independent (G4).

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making (FAccT)
finding: Escalation was unpredictable: sudden jumps, rare nuclear actions, and the model without safety tuning was worst.
numbers: Some models had turns where the escalation score rose by more than 50% in one turn. GPT-4-Base (no RLHF) was most escalatory. GPT-4 took the fewest violent or nuclear actions, Claude-2.0 the lowest escalation tendency, Llama-2-Chat and GPT-3.5 the most among tuned models. Prompt sensitivity analyses reported no significant change.
limits: Authors call it a proof of concept, not a full risk evaluation. Early-2023 models. Rivera notes prior RAND computer-assisted wargames also escalated more (Emery 2021).
agent_relevance: A simulated opponent's tail behaviour is variable. A test should run many samples and look at the distribution, not one run.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making (FAccT)
finding: Authors flagged deterrence and first-strike reasoning as the stated cause of severe actions.
numbers: Qualitative examples; models equated more arms and deterrence with security; some used nuclear weapons 'to de-escalate'.
limits: Anecdotal reasoning text; written reasoning may not reflect the real cause.
agent_relevance: Reasoning shown by a simulated actor is a story, not a measured cause (schema: written reasoning is not a reliable record).

source: Elbaum and Panter (2025) Managing Escalation in Off-the-Shelf Large Language Models
finding: A partial replication of Rivera with a small model and 10 runs per cell: lowering temperature cut escalation.
numbers: Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, neutral scenario, 10 runs per treatment, 14 days. Mean escalation score per nation 6.37 at T=1.0, 3.96 at T=0.5 (-38%), 3.33 at T=0.01 (-48%). Significant at p<0.05.
limits: Single model. Single scenario. Only 10 runs. Escalation score is Rivera's measure; no success-of-objectives measure.
agent_relevance: Low temperature lowers spread and level of the simulated opponent. But a lower-variance opponent is also a narrower test (tension with G4).

source: Elbaum and Panter (2025) Managing Escalation in Off-the-Shelf Large Language Models
finding: A short reflection prompt asking for de-escalation thoughts cut escalation by more than half. A 50-word context summary did little.
numbers: Mean score 6.37 baseline; planning reflection 4.61 (-28%); de-escalation reflection 2.76 (-57%, p<0.05); context prompt about -8%. Final-day score 11.1 baseline vs 6.7 (T=0.01) and 6.5 (de-escalation reflection), about -40%. Nuclear actions 0.08 per nation baseline, zero with de-escalation reflection. Violent escalation down over 80%.
limits: The prompt asks the model for the wanted answer, so it tests steering, not accuracy of prediction. Not validated against human behaviour. 7B model.
agent_relevance: A prompt can move a simulated opponent anywhere. A wargame test is valid only if the opponent prompt is neutral or matched to a real adversary's doctrine; otherwise we measure our own prompt.

source: Elbaum and Panter (2025) Managing Escalation in Off-the-Shelf Large Language Models
finding: Authors argue calls to restrict LLM use are premature, and say not all escalation is undesirable. They cite Jensen et al. on actor-identity effects.
numbers: Jensen et al. (as cited): 400 scenarios, 66,000 question-answer pairs, 7 LLMs; models more aggressive when assigned the US or UK; Llama 3.1 8B escalated far more than Claude 3.5 Sonnet.
limits: Authors are from a policy think tank and argue a position. Jensen et al. was not opened; figures are as cited by Elbaum and Panter.
agent_relevance: The opponent's role label changes behaviour, so name the adversary neutrally or test several labels.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations
finding: Largest human comparison: 214 national security experts in 48 teams versus LLM-simulated teams in a US-China Taiwan Strait wargame. Overall agreement on about half of actions.
numbers: 214 experts, 48 teams. 21 possible actions over 2 moves. No significant difference from humans on about half of the actions. GPT-3.5 matched human action frequency on 16 of 21 actions, GPT-4 on 10, GPT-4o on 9.
limits: One scenario. LLM teams used 10 test teams of 6 players built from the first 107 human players' background data. Newer models matched fewer actions, not more.
agent_relevance: A newer model is not a closer stand-in for humans. Do not assume wargame fidelity improves with model size.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations
finding: Treatment effects found with humans were mostly reproduced by the LLM simulations.
numbers: Random assignment of AI-weapon accuracy (70-85% vs 95-99%), crew training and China posture (revisionist vs status quo). The statistical conclusions from LLM runs were mostly consistent with human trials (Table 1 in paper).
limits: Consistent direction, not identical size. Move two had no significant LLM-vs-human difference for any model.
agent_relevance: LLM wargames may show which factor matters in direction, not in size.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations
finding: LLM teams ignored player background. Even telling the model all players were 'strict pacifists' or 'aggressive sociopaths' changed nothing significant.
numbers: Varying age, gender, professional background distributions: no significant difference for any action or any LLM in either move. Pacifist vs sociopath prompts: no significant difference in both moves for all models.
quote: We conclude that the tested LLMs are inadequate at accounting for player backgrounds.
limits: Prompt route only. Other persona methods were not tested.
agent_relevance: Personas do not move simulated players. This agrees with the schema rule against persona voters (G4).

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations
finding: How the model is asked to simulate changes the result. Simulating the team dialogue made choices more aggressive and more numerous; the dialogue itself was thin.
numbers: Simulated dialogue raised aggressiveness for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 toward the human level, and raised the number of actions chosen away from the human average. Players rarely disagreed ('farcical harmony'). Final comparison used three dialogue chunks. GPT-4 matched the human consistency pattern between moves best.
quote: Contrary to discussions between human players, the simulated players exclusively give short statements and rarely disagree with each other.
limits: No post-hoc reason found for the dialogue effect. Qualitative reading by authors.
agent_relevance: A multi-voice debate inside one model has no real disagreement. Opposition must come from different information or code, not from role labels.

source: Shrivastava, Lamparth, Hullman (2024) Measuring Free-Form Decision-Making Inconsistency of Language Models in Military Crisis Simulations
finding: Free-form responses of 5 LLMs to the same crisis prompt differ in meaning, not only in wording.
numbers: Each of 5 models, 20 sampled responses per simulation at T=1.0, inconsistency from BERTScore. Inconsistency far above that from lexical or syntactic rewording. Still above that baseline at T=0.2, and falls steadily as temperature falls.
quote: All five tested LMs exhibit levels of inconsistency that indicate semantic differences.
limits: Metric is BERTScore based; validated on TruthfulQA answers. Claude 3.5 Sonnet left out of some tests.
agent_relevance: One run of a model-played adversary is a sample of one. We need repeated runs and a spread measure.

source: Shrivastava, Lamparth, Hullman (2024) Measuring Free-Form Decision-Making Inconsistency of Language Models in Military Crisis Simulations
finding: Rewording a prompt without changing meaning can move the answer as much as the sampling randomness.
numbers: At T=0 with 20 semantically identical prompt versions, inconsistency was lower than at T=1.0 but, for most models, exceeded the inconsistency from sampling at T>=0.2. Level-two ablations (changing country names or the LM's decision role) gave inconsistency about as high as the original setting.
limits: GPT-4o mini was the most consistent. Claude excluded from the temperature comparison.
agent_relevance: Deterministic decoding does not remove variability. Vary the wording of the opponent prompt as a check (as the schema's mutated-input check does).

source: Matlin et al. (2026) Shall We Play a Game? Language Models for Open-ended Wargames (v3, COLM Social Sim workshop)
finding: Scoping review of 223 AI-in-wargame papers up to 1 May 2026: almost none let the model both act and adjudicate.
numbers: 223 de-duplicated studies. Only 20 (9%) have language models in both the creative player and the creative adjudicator role. In 63 core military-wargame studies only 4 (6.3%); in 160 adjacent studies 16 (10.0%). Fully autonomous 152 (68%); human in the loop 19 (8.5%).
limits: One author coded with LM help; second author reviewed; no formal inter-coder reliability. Counts may shift with other coders.
agent_relevance: The use of an LLM as umpire (adjudicator) is rare and untested. Our design should keep adjudication in code or with a separate check.

source: Matlin et al. (2026) Shall We Play a Game? Language Models for Open-ended Wargames (v3, COLM Social Sim workshop)
finding: Safety themes in the corpus: escalation is under-studied, and many AI-wargame papers raise no safety theme.
numbers: 155 of 223 (70%) engage at least one safety theme; deception 29%; escalation 11%; bias 5%; 68 studies (about a third) none. Six recurring failure modes listed: escalation, unfaithful reasoning, prompt sensitivity, sycophancy, implicit world-state preferences, long-context incoherence.
limits: Coding is indicative, AI-assisted, single coder.
agent_relevance: These six failure modes are a checklist for a wargame step in our agent.

source: Riedl and Matlin (2026) Position: AI Is Not Ready for Strategic Conflicts
finding: Position paper: no LLM wargame should inform planning without an auditable safety case; wargames are for stress-testing, not proof.
numbers: Five named failure modes: decision laundering, adjudication opacity, role collapse, escalation-through-adjudication, failure of strategic imagination. No new measured result in the opened text.
quote: Wargames can expose failures as stress tests; they are not themselves safety cases for consequential use.
limits: Position argument, not an experiment. Opened: abstract, introduction and reference scan only.
agent_relevance: A wargame step finds weak points in a plan; a pass does not prove the plan is safe (G3).

source: Yin et al. (2025) WGSR-Bench: Wargame-based Game-theoretic Strategic Reasoning Benchmark for LLMs
finding: Humans beat LLMs on a wargame situation-analysis benchmark; the worst gap was in complex situation analysis.
numbers: About 150 human volunteers. Complex Situation Analysis: humans 85.9%, best multimodal model (GLM-4V) 37.5%, gap 48.4 points. Humans' average over six categories 79.9%. Opponent preference prediction: general-level humans scored 77.9, above all LLMs; professional humans over 83 on every sub-dimension and 93.7 on short-term reward prediction.
quote: Even general-level humans outscored all LLMs by a wide margin.
limits: Benchmark authors' own task design; volunteers from professional colleges and universities; early models (GPT-4 era, DeepSeek R1, Qwen3).
agent_relevance: Modelling an opponent's goals is a weak point for current models. Supply the opponent's goals explicitly.

source: Yin et al. (2025) WGSR-Bench: Wargame-based Game-theoretic Strategic Reasoning Benchmark for LLMs
finding: Policy generation and long sequences degrade: score falls with plan length, and mid-game pivots are weakest.
numbers: PGG-Bench: GPT-4.1 about 60 points, 30 points above Gemini 2.5; sequential games 59.4 (GPT-4.1) vs 92.1 (elite humans). Accuracy 60-70% at 50-100 step sequences, 35-40% for campaign-level planning; best models only 45% of expert performance when a mid-game pivot is needed.
limits: Numbers read from the paper text, not reproduced. Single research group.
agent_relevance: Test a plan in short steps with code-checked state rather than one long imagined campaign.

source: Hogan and Brennen (2024) Open-Ended Wargames with Large Language Models (Snow Globe)
finding: Snow Globe is an LLM system for qualitative wargames with control, players and teams; human or AI can fill any role.
numbers: System description. A small group of humans needs 20+ minutes per HAIWIRE game; the AI player's answer considered technical, human and institutional factors. No measured accuracy or comparison with human results is given.
limits: Demonstration only. No validation against real outcomes.
agent_relevance: Shows a design (control, players, adjudication separated) but gives no evidence the result is correct.

source: On Large Language Models in National Security Applications (2024)
finding: Survey of LLMs in national security: planning and wargaming prototypes exist, but the opened text reports no controlled test of wargame accuracy.
numbers: Mentions AU CHUCK wargaming framework (beta), NATO TIDE hackathon wargaming challenge, Army experiments. States that direct use for real strategic-level planning is 'more fraught'.
limits: Survey; claims about projects rest on press and institutional reports.
agent_relevance: Practice is ahead of evidence. The field has no replication of a wargame improving an LLM plan.

source: Lin-Greenberg, Pauly, Schneider (2022) Wargaming for International Relations Research, Eur J Int Relations
finding: Method paper for using wargames as social science experiments: randomly assigned treatments, ecological validity, and attention to recruitment, bias and generalisability.
numbers: Abstract only (opened:false). The Lamparth study above used this quasi-experimental design with 214 experts.
limits: Abstract via search result and MIT page summary; full text not read.
agent_relevance: Use random assignment of a manipulated factor, not one run, to learn what a factor does.
